q-50865.name: Question 1
q-50865.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{4n}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=0$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
q-50865.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{4n}=\frac{x}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}+⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{x}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+⋯.
$$

The Taylor series for the function f(x) about x=0 is given by f(x)=∑n=1∞xn4n. Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about x=0 of f′(x).

a
f′(x)=1+x2+x24+⋯
b
f′(x)=14+x4+x24+⋯
c
f′(x)=18−x8+x28−⋯
d
f′(x)=x4+x28+x312+⋯
e
f′(x)=12+x2+x22+⋯
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

∑n=1∞xn4n=x4+x28+x312+⋯.

To find f′(x), we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

f′(x)=14+x4+x24+⋯.

q-347640.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=0$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$

${f}^{′}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
$-\,{x}^{3}+\,⋯$
q-347640.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}{x}^{n}=x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=1-x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}+⋯.
$$

q-126105.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(2n-1)!}(x-2)^{2n}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=2$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
q-126105.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(2n-1)!}(x-2)^{2n}=-(x-2)^{2}+\frac{1}{6}(x-2)^{4}-\frac{1}{120}(x-2)^{6}+⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-2(x-2)+\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{3}-\frac{1}{20}(x-2)^{5}+⋯.
$$

Question 3
?

The Taylor series for the function f(x) about x=2 is given by f(x)=∑n=1∞(−1)n(2n−1)!(x−2)2n. Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about x=2 of f′(x).

a
f′(x)=−(x−2)+13(x−2)3−19(x−2)5+⋯
b
f′(x)=−2(x−2)+15(x−2)3−120(x−2)5+⋯
c
f′(x)=−(x−2)+14(x−2)3−19(x−2)5+⋯
d
f′(x)=−2(x−2)+23(x−2)3−49(x−2)5+⋯
e
f′(x)=−2(x−2)+23(x−2)3−120(x−2)5+⋯
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have f(x)=∑n=1∞(−1)n(2n−1)!(x−2)2n=−(x−2)2+16(x−2)4−1120(x−2)6+⋯.

To find f′(x), we differentiate term-by-term. This gives f′(x)=−2(x−2)+23(x−2)3−120(x−2)5+⋯.

q-50863.name: Question 4
q-50863.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{3n}{x}^{n-1}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=0$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
q-50863.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{3n}{x}^{n-1}=-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}x-\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{12}{x}^{3}-⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=0+\frac{1}{6}-\frac{2}{9}x+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}-⋯.
$$

q-352520.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by 

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n}}{(2n+1)!}.
$$

Find the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x).$

${f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }$
{{field-1}}
$(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n-1}$
q-352520.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
f(x)=\frac{x}{6}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{120}+⋯+{{\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n}}{(2n+1)!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{6}-\frac{2x}{120}+⋯+{{\frac{(-1)^{n+1}n{x}^{n-1}}{(2n+1)!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n-1}}{(2n+1)!} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{(2n+1)!}(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

q-126164.name: Question 9
q-126164.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by 

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2n+1}}{n}.
$$

Find ${a}_{n},$ given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.
$$
q-126164.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
f(x)={x}^{3}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{2}+⋯+{{\frac{{x}^{2n+1}}{n}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+\frac{5{x}^{4}}{2}+⋯+{{\frac{(2n+1){x}^{2n}}{n}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(2n+1){x}^{2n}}{n}
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(2n+1){x}^{2n}}{n}.
$$

q-50910.name: Question 11
q-50910.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n!}{x}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the Taylor series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
q-50910.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$ 

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot \frac{n!}{(-1)^{n-1}{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)x\cdot n!}{(n+1)!}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{|x|}{n+1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges when $L<1.$  Since $0<1$ for all $x,$ we conclude that 
$R=\infty .$
